nodes.text: Sato et al. 2014, overview of Y-chromosome variation in modern Japanese males.
D1a2a/D-M55 persists at high frequency in modern Japanese male lineages.
Paternal-lineage asymmetry may indicate some form of social or reproductive advantage for Jomon-associated paternal lineages.
D1a2a/D-M55 persistence is best understood as passive Jomon-associated survival.
Hudson 1992 on Yayoi ritual and dotaku context.
Dotaku ritual flourished and then ended in the Late Yayoi period.
The end of dotaku ritual may reflect social reorganization or network disruption, not solely internal cultural transformation.
Dotaku discontinuity is usually treated as internal ritual transformation or cultural transition.
Kiki myths may preserve structures of ritual-political memory related to social integration.
Y-chromosome frequency alone cannot prove conquest or elite dominance.
If representative Kofun elite burials do not show elevated D1a2a/D-M55 compared with non-elites, the paternal-elite version is weakened.
Comparative cases are possibility structures, not evidence for the Japanese case.

edges.reason: P1 supports the Y-lineage frequency observation.
Frequency asymmetry is consistent with, but does not prove, social advantage.
The claim reframes passive survival as possible social signal.
R1 limits the strength of UC1.
F1 gives a test that could weaken UC1.
Dotaku discontinuity allows but does not prove social reorganization.
UC2 introduces an alternative to purely internal transformation.
Comparative cases can frame possibility but not prove UC2.
